f.c:
Directions: This question is based on the seven accompanying documents. The documents have been edited for the purpose of this exercise.

 

Document 1

Source: “A Patriotic Song,” the Aberdeen Journal, Scotland, ca. 1805

Come all ye gallant Scottish swains [young men],

From town and cottage, hills and plains,

Let every village beat to arms,

And join the warlike quorum [assembly].

 

For Bonaparte he’ll be here,

Bonaparte, Bonaparte,

For Bonaparte he’ll be here,

The great devil choke him.

 

For Bonaparte he’ll be here,

He will not leave us horse or mare,

He’ll take our other going gear,

And drive them all before him.

 

But let us true and faithful stand,

Heart to heart, and hand to hand,

When the rascals try to land,

We shall be there before ’em.

 

Why does this corrupt usurper boast,

That he’ll invade our British coast,

We’ll show him Soldiers to his cost,

Was born long before him.

 

He’ll find our courage still the same,

We’ll turn his glory to his shame,

Our old Claymore [sword] we’ll try again,

And highland blood devour him.

Document 2

Source: Letter from Pope Pius VII to Napoleon, 1806

Your Majesty lays down the principle that you are the Emperor of Rome. I reply, with apostolic frankness, that the Pope, who became Sovereign of Rome so many centuries ago that no other sovereignty on earth can go back to a more remote point in history, does not acknowledge, and never has acknowledged, any power superior to himself in his own dominions. Your Majesty is immensely great; you have been elected, crowned, consecrated, and acknowledged, as Emperor of the French, but not as Emperor of Rome.

Document 3

Source: Letter from Napoleon to the Emperor of Austria, October 1808

Sire, my Brother:

I had it in my power to dismember your Majesty’s monarchy, or at least to diminish its power. I did not do so. It exists as it is by my consent. This is a plain proof that our accounts are settled; that I have no desire to injure you. I am always ready to guarantee the integrity of your monarchy. I will never do anything adverse to the important interests of States. But your Majesty ought not to bring again under discussion what has been settled by a fifteen years’ war. You ought to avoid every proclamation or act calculated to lead to war.

Document 4

Source: Anonymous Russian nun, account of the French occupation of Moscow, 1812

They slept in the sanctuary, they ate off the altar. In the hospital church there was a large icon representing the appearances of the Mother of God, painted on wood and without fittings. One of our elderly sisters had bought it with her own money and presented it to the church. The French took it from the wall and used it as a table. We were extremely upset to find that they had no respect for our churches, and our chaplain said to us: “How do you expect them to revere churches which have been turned into dwelling-places. If they sin through ignorance, God will forgive them, because they have not profaned any holy relics.”

Document 5

Source: Twelve princesses of the House of Hohenzollern, led by princess Marianne of Prussia, “Appeal to the Women of the Prussian State,” March 1813

We women, too, must participate, and must help promote victory. We, too, must unite with the men and boys to save our fatherland. Thus let us found an association with the name of Women’s Association for the Good of the Fatherland.

This association will accept as donations not merely cash money, but any valuable spare trinket . . . Monthly contributions, material, linen cloth, spun wool and yarn will be gladly accepted, and even the working of these raw materials without pay will be regarded as an offering. These offerings serve to arm, clothe and equip the defenders who need it, and if the rich benevolence of women puts us in a position to do yet more, then the wounded will also be nursed, healed and returned to the grateful fatherland.

Document 6

Source: Dutch cartoon, “Napoleon in the Press,” printed during the allied campaign against Napoleon after his 1812 defeat in Russia, 1813

 
 

Soldiers of the Allied nations squeeze Napoleon in a press, as the names of various liberated countries, including Holland, spill from his mouth.

Document 7

Source: Memorandum by the Piedmontese ambassador, Count Cotti di Brusasco, to the Tsar Alexander, March 1818

By one of those despotic caprices with which he appeared to delight in affronting accepted notions and doing violence to nature, Bonaparte had decided to make several millions of Italians into Frenchmen—first the Piedmontese*, then the Genoese*, then the Tuscans* and finally the Romans*. An artificial line now separated the populations who were intended by their topographical position, by their language and common origins, by nature itself, to form a single nation. Bonaparte imagined he could level the Alps, or rather transport them to his arbitrary line . . . by simple decree. The whole of French Italy was peopled with French employees, from the chief officer of police to the lowliest tax collector.

*Inhabitants of various regions of northern and central Italy

Evaluate whether the French Revolution was motivated primarily by Enlightenment ideas or by economic concerns.

f.c:
Directions: This question is based on the seven accompanying documents. The documents have been edited for the purpose of this exercise.

 
 

Document 1

Source: François-Noël Babeuf, French tax collector, private letter to his friend Dubois de Fosseux, 1787

Must there be any distinctions at all between men? Why give any greater dignity to him who carries a sword [traditional symbol of the nobility] than to him who forges it? Did Nature, who gave predominance to our species, command that it submit to other laws than those drawn up for all the other species of animate beings? Did it desire that one individual be less well-fed, less well-clothed and less well-housed than another? Is it likely that this is the way things were done in the earliest ages of life on earth? Our most advanced knowledge of what were the natural customs of our brothers, the American Indians, before we discovered their peaceful country and began treating them so poorly, certainly would disprove any assertion to that effect.

Document 2

Source: List of grievances from members of the Third Estate* living in the town of Carcassonne, southern France, early 1789

A holy respect for religion, morality, civil liberty, and the rights of property, a speedy return to true principles, a careful selection and due measure in the matter of the taxes, a strict proportionality in their assessment, a persistent economy in government expenditures, and indispensable reforms in all branches of the administration, are the best and perhaps the only means of perpetuating the existence of the monarchy.

Therefore, the third estate of the electoral district of Carcassonne very humbly petitions his Majesty to take into consideration these concerns, weigh them in his wisdom, and permit his people to enjoy, as soon as may be, fresh proofs of his benevolence.

*Term used in pre-revolutionary France to refer to all people who were not part of the clergy (the First Estate) or the nobility (the Second Estate)

Document 3

Source: List of grievances issued by members of the French clergy, early 1789

The salt tax and the various sales taxes ought to be suppressed, or replaced, if need be, with a tax less burdensome.

Customs duties should be limited to goods crossing the frontiers of France.

Registry fees* have grown to an exorbitant figure. The irregularity of these charges from place to place creates frequent contentions.

It is desirable to lessen the disadvantage under which poor country people labor in securing justice in the matter of over-taxation, on account of the considerable expense of bringing their cases to court.

The shifting of certain taxes might bring them to bear upon various articles of luxury, and especially upon unnecessary articles of domestic use.

*Legal fees charged for various transactions

Document 4

Source: Anonymous political cartoon, “Awakening of the Third Estate,” early 1789

The figure on the left represents the nobility. The figure in the center represents the clergy. The figure on the ground represents the Third Estate, a term used before the revolution to identify all people in France who were not part of the clergy or the nobility.

Translation of caption: “My goodness, it was time I woke up. My chains were giving me nightmares.”

Document 5

Source: Jacques Antoine Creuzé-Latouche, French lawyer, account of the king’s reform proposals presented to the Estates General, 1789

The “Declaration of the King’s Intentions” made up the most bizarre, the most despotic, the most contradictory set of instructions ever to be found in history: the king annulled all limitation on his powers, and prohibited the establishment of any future limitations. He desired that all property rights should be observed, such as church tithes [taxes paid to the Catholic church], dues owed to noble landowners, feudal rights, etc. In fact, he had drawn up the constitution by himself. Some features of these arrangements which favored the clergy and the nobility were greeted by them with cries of “Long live the king!” while there was unbroken silence and no response from the deputies of the Third Estate.

Document 6

Source: French newspaper, report, July 1789

The nearer July 14th came, the greater became the shortage of food. The crowd, besieging every baker’s shop, received a small distribution of bread, always with warnings about possible shortages the next day. Fears were redoubled by the complaints of people who had spent the whole day waiting at the baker’s door without receiving anything.

As I was forced at the height of the shortage to go to Versailles for a short visit, I was curious to see what sort of bread was being eaten at court, or served at the ministers’ and deputies’ tables. Nowhere could I find even rye bread. Everywhere I saw only beautiful bread, of the finest and most delicate quality. It was served in great abundance and delivered by the bakers themselves.

Document 7

Source: Women’s petition to the National Assembly, October 1789

It is astonishing that, having gone so far along the path of reforms, and having cut down much of the forest of prejudices, you would leave standing the oldest and most general of all abuses, the one which excludes half of the inhabitants of this vast kingdom from positions, dignities, honors, and especially from the right to sit amongst you.

You have generously decreed equality of rights for all; you have made the humble march alongside the princes and lords of the earth. At last, thanks to your good influence, a serene day will break above our heads, a new people, of citizens, wise and happy, will raise itself on the ruins.

Will women then be the only ones for whom the iron age of oppression will forever continue?

Learning Objective: Explain the causes, events, and consequences of the French Revolution.
Thematic Focus: European states and nations developed governmental and civil institutions from 1450 to the present to organize society and consolidate political power, with a variety of social, cultural, and economic effects.
Historical Development: The French Revolution resulted from a combination of long-term social and political causes, as well as Enlightenment ideas, exacerbated by short-term fiscal and economic crises.

Directions: This question is based on the seven accompanying documents. The documents have been edited for the purpose of this exercise.

 
 

Document 1

Source: Jacques Necker, finance minister, confidential report to the king, 1781

A significant difference between annual spending and annual revenue will soon result in great inconveniences, since the deficit can only be dealt with by loans, and the interest owed on these loans results in a daily worsening of the problem. [To meet our increased military expenditures] public credit has been attacked, indeed almost destroyed, by the several government cancellations both of principal and interest, and by frequent delay of payment.

Document 2

Source: Petition by women of the Third Estate* to the king, January 1789

The women of the Third Estate are almost all born without wealth; their education is very neglected or very defective.

To prevent so many ills, Sire, we ask that men not be allowed, under any pretext, to exercise trades that are the prerogative of women—whether as seamstress, embroiderer, millinery shopkeeper, etc., etc. We implore you, Sire, to set up free schools where we might learn the basis of religion and ethics. May our hearts be formed there; may we be taught above all to practice the virtues of women: gentleness, modesty, patience, charity.

We ask to be educated, and to have work, not to usurp men’s authority, but to be better esteemed by them, and so that we might have the means of living safe from misfortune.

*term used before the revolution to identify all people in France who were not part of the clergy or the nobility

Document 3

Source: French political cartoon showing a figure representing the Third Estate carrying the First and Second Estates while rabbits and birds eat his harvest, early 1789

 
 
 
 
 

Translation of the caption: “One must hope that this game will end soon.”

Document 4

Source: Decree of the National Assembly, August 1789

The National Assembly hereby completely abolishes the feudal system. It decrees that, among the existing rights and dues, all those originating in or representing real or personal serfdom or personal servitude, shall be abolished without compensation.

Because a national constitution and public liberty are of more advantage to the provinces than the privileges which some of these provinces enjoy, and because the surrender of such privileges is essential to the closer union of all parts of the realm, all the provincial privileges and tax exemptions, are once for all abolished and are absorbed into the law common to all Frenchmen.

All citizens, without distinction of birth, are eligible to any office or dignity, whether ecclesiastical, civil or military; and no profession shall imply any inferiority.

Document 5

Source: Address presented to the National Assembly by a delegation of Jews living in Paris, August 1789*

The Jews residing in Paris, filled with admiration and respect at the sight of the many acts of justice emanating from the National Assembly, have dared flatter themselves that their lot will not escape your attention; that they too will feel the happy effects of your wisdom.

We would like to think that your justice doesn’t ask to be solicited or called upon by our wishes. In restoring to man his original dignity, in reestablishing him in the enjoyment of his rights, it was not your intention to make any distinction between one man and another. This title belongs to all members of society, and the rights that flow from it thus belong to us equally.

*Jews living in France before 1789 faced numerous residential and occupational restrictions.

Document 6

Source: Jean-Paul Marat, French journalist and politician, newspaper article, September 1789

I beseech my readers to observe that in refusing to enforce the decree regulating the movement and export of grain, the king and his ministers are seeking to find a means of continuing their monopoly, and of breaking the people by famine.

Again I beseech my readers to observe that, in pressing for financial reform measures, they are only awaiting the time when the public treasury is filled again, at which time they can stop the work of the National Assembly, and reduce to nothing the great work of the Constitution, and return the people to their chains.

Here is the nation, itself enchained by its representatives and delivered defenseless to an arrogant master who, forgetful of his powerlessness, violates his promises and oaths.

Document 7

Source: Frenchwomen Freed, French engraving, early 1790s

 
 
 

The woman is wearing revolutionary symbols and carrying a spear marked with the words “Liberty or Death.”

Directions: This question is based on the seven accompanying documents. The documents have been edited for the purpose of this exercise.

 
 

Document 1

Source: Arthur Young, British agricultural expert, diary of his travels in France in the late 1780s

JUNE 1, 1787. The same wretched country continues; the fields are scenes of disgraceful management. Yet all this farmland could be improved, if they knew what to do with it: Heaven grant me patience while I see a country thus neglected—and forgive me the oaths I swear at the absence and ignorance of the landlords.

JUNE 10. Met many beggars, which we had not done before. All the country girls and women are without shoes or stockings; and the ploughmen at their work do not have clogs. This is poverty that strikes at the root of national prosperity.

Document 2

Source: Charles, Count de Calonne, proposals presented to the Assembly of Notables [a group of French noblemen called together by the king to enact financial reforms], 1787

Tax exemptions are defended by self-interest, influence, wealth and ancient prejudices which seem to be hallowed by time. But what are all these together compared with the common good and the necessity of the state? These abuses oppress the wealth-producing, laboring class. Unjust tax exemptions only relieve one section of taxpayers by aggravating the condition of the others.

His Majesty has decided to remedy these defects by applying the rules of a strictly distributive justice, by restoring the original intention behind the vingtième tax [a type of income tax], and by raising it to its true value without increasing anyone’s contribution, and finally by abolishing every kind of tax exemption. The vingtième will be replaced by a general land tax, covering the whole area of the kingdom.

Document 3

Source: Jean-Sylvain Bailly, mayor of Paris and member of the National Assembly, recalling events in early 1789

In the district assembly, I felt that I breathed a new air. It was a marvel to be something in the political system, and that merely by virtue of being a citizen, or rather a burgess [prominent resident] of Paris, for at that time we were still burgesses, not citizens.

The men who for years had been meeting in the clubs used to discuss public affairs in them, but only as topics of conversation. They had no rights, no influence whatever.

Here, we had an influence—distant, certainly, but obtained for the first time in more than a century and a half. This assembly was conscious of the rights and strength of the whole. It realized that these rights and this strength lent it a kind of authority, one that may reside in the wills of individuals who are destined to form the general will.

Document 4

Source: List of grievances by anonymous women, early 1789

We have a right to complain about the education we are given, about the prejudices that make us slaves, and about the injustice with which we are deprived at birth of the inheritances that nature and equity should assure us.

Could it be possible that philosophy would be mute with regard to our situation, or rather that men, deaf to its voice and insensitive to its light, would persist in rendering us victims of their pride and injustice?

We do not aspire to the honors of government, or to the advantages of being initiated to the secrets of ministries. But we believe that it is just to count the votes of women, because they are obligated, just as are men, to pay the royal taxes and to fulfill the engagements of commerce.

Document 5

Source: Emmanuel-Joseph Sieyès, clergyman and political theorist, “What Is the Third Estate*?” pamphlet, early 1789

The pretended usefulness of a privileged order [the nobility] for the public service is nothing more than a myth. Without the privileged order, high government offices would be infinitely better filled; because these offices naturally ought to go to those of ability and recognized service. If privileged persons have come to usurp all the lucrative and honorable offices, it is a hateful injustice to the rank and file of citizens and at the same time a treason to the public good.

Privileged persons, far from being useful to the nation, can only enfeeble and injure it. The noble order does not enter at all into the social organization; it may indeed be a burden upon the nation, and it cannot of itself constitute a nation.

*Term used before the revolution to identify all people in France who were not part of the clergy (the First Estate) or the nobility (the Second Estate)

Document 6

Source: “He was only wishing us well,”* anonymous satirical cartoon, November 1789

 
 

*The title of the cartoon is a pun in French that can also be read as saying “He only wanted our property.”

The figure in the center is a Roman Catholic bishop. The figure in black is a church official counting money at a table.

Document 7

Source: Nicolas de Condorcet, “On the Admission of Women to the Rights of Citizenship,” pamphlet, July 1790

Habit can familiarize men with the violation of their natural rights to the point that, among those who have lost them, no one dreams of reclaiming them or believes that he has suffered an injustice.

For this exclusion not to be an act of tyranny one would have to prove that the natural rights of women are not absolutely the same as those of men or show that they are not capable of exercising them. Now the rights of men follow only from the fact that they are feeling beings, capable of acquiring moral ideas and of reasoning about these ideas. Since women have the same qualities, they necessarily have equal rights. Either no individual in mankind has true rights, or all have the same ones.

f.c:
Directions: This question is based on the seven accompanying documents. The documents have been edited for the purpose of this exercise.

 

Document 1

Source: Martin Luther, The Blessed Sacrament of the Holy and True Body of Christ and the Brotherhoods, 1519

If men desire to maintain a brotherhood*, they should gather provisions and feed a tableful or two of poor people, for the sake of God. On the feast day they should remain sober, passing the time in prayer and other good works. Or they should gather the money which they intend to squander for drink, and collect it into a common treasury. Then in cases of hardship, needy fellow workmen might be helped to get started, and be lent money, or a young couple might be fitted out respectably from this common treasury. These would be works of true brotherhood; they would make God and his saints look with favor upon the brotherhoods, of which they would then gladly be the patrons.

* A voluntary association of lay people created for the purpose of promoting special works of Christian charity or piety

Document 2

Source: Illustration by Lucas Cranach the Elder, included in a pamphlet by Martin Luther, 1521

 
 

The images contrast Christ washing his disciples’ feet with the Pope having his feet kissed.

Document 3

Source: Andreas Karlstadt, Protestant theologian at the University of Wittenberg, On the Removal of Images, 1522

1. To have images in churches and houses of God is wrong and contrary to the first commandment given by God, “You shall have no other gods before me”.

2. To have carved or painted idols upon altars is more harmful and devilish still.

3. It is good, necessary, praiseworthy, and godly to do away with them and to give the reasons found in Scripture for their removal.

All who worship God through images worship falsehood. They are focusing on the appearance and external signs of God. Yet, their heart is far from God, creating its own idol in the heart and being full of lies.

Document 4

Source: Robert Parkyn, Catholic priest, commentary on the English Reformation, compiled 1532–1546

In many places of this realm neither bread nor water was sanctified or distributed among Christian people on Sunday, but clearly omitted as things tending to idolatry. Yea, and also the sacred vessels hanging over the altars (wherein was remaining Christ’s blessed body under form of bread) was spitefully cast away as things most abominable, and did not pass of the blessed hosts therein contained, but villainously despised them, uttering such words thereby as it did abhor true Christian ears for to hear.

Document 5

Source: John Calvin, biblical commentary, 1546

In so far as a wife is a help to her husband, so as to make his life happy, that is in accordance with God’s institution. For in the beginning God appointed it that the man without the woman was, as it were, but half a man, and felt himself destitute of special and necessary assistance, and the wife is, as it were, the completing of the man. Sin afterwards came in to corrupt that institution of God; for in place of so great a blessing there has been substituted a grievous punishment, so that marriage is the source and occasion of many miseries. Hence, whatever evil or inconvenience there is in marriage, that evil arises from the corruption of the divine institution.

Document 6

Source: Testimony of Anne Askew, executed for professing radical Protestant beliefs during the reign of Henry VIII in England, 1546

Then the bishop’s representative rebuked me, and said, that I was much to blame for uttering the scriptures. For St. Paul (he said) forbade women to speak or talk of the word of God. I answered him that I knew Paul’s meaning as well as he, which is in 1 Corinthians 14, that a woman ought not to speak in the congregation by the way of teaching. And then I asked him, how many women he had seen go into the pulpit and preach? He said he never saw none. Then I said, he ought to find no fault in poor women, except that they had offended the law.

Document 7

Source: Ordinance [law] of the Protestant Danish city of Malmø, 1549

First it was gravely determined, decided and agreed upon that no one should be sitting and drinking alcohol during the sermon on Sundays or other holy days, nor should anyone wander around in the street or in the chapel behind the choir during the sermon. Nor should any drinking establishment be opened on aforesaid days before the noonday sermon is over, unless it is done for the sake of strangers and travelers who arrive and want to leave at once. Whoever breaks this rule will be punished accordingly.

Similarly, all single men and unemployed manservants should swear an oath to Council acting on behalf of His Royal Majesty and the city of Malmø or they should be expelled from the city.

Similarly, all girls who are self-supporting should enter into service again or be expelled from the city at once.

Directions: This question is based on the seven accompanying documents. The documents have been edited for the purpose of this exercise.

 

Document 1

Source: Catholic emperor Charles V, message to his council, 1521

I am descended from the most Christian emperors of the noble German nation, from the Catholic kings of Spain, the archdukes of Austria and the dukes of Burgundy. I am determined to support everything that these predecessors and I myself have kept. For it is certain that a single friar [Martin Luther] errs in his opinion which is against all of Christendom, and according to which all of Christianity has been in error both in the past thousand years and even more in the present. For that reason I am absolutely determined to stake on this cause my kingdoms and territories, my friends, my body and blood, my life and soul. I declare to you that I regret having so long delayed to proceed against this Luther and his false doctrine and I am no longer willing to hear him speak more, but I am making it clear that immediately, he be taken back without preaching or admonishing the people with his bad doctrine, and making sure that no disorder results.

Document 2

Source: Protestant destruction of icons [artistic representations of Christ and the saints] in Zurich, Switzerland, 1524

 

Document 3

Source: Martin Luther, A Sermon on Marriage, 1525

The wife veils herself with a fine, soft veil, spun and sewn out of pretty, soft flax or linen. Why does she do this? So that she speaks fine, lovely, friendly words to her husband and not coarse, filthy, scolding words, as the bad wives do who carry a sword in their mouths. Therefore, the wife should have the manner of a grapevine, as it says in the 128th Psalm, for this lets itself be bent and directed with a little band of straw, as the winemaker desires. Just so should wives let themselves be guided and taught by their husbands.

That is now what the wife should do in marriage, namely, that she should be subordinate and obedient to her husband and not undertake or do anything without his consent.

Document 4

Source: Valerius Anshelm, Protestant Swiss chronicler of the German Peasant War, 1525

In sum, what the peasants and their supporters undertook, namely, to free the Gospel and themselves through rebellion, was itself overthrown by rebellion, so that evangelical teaching and preaching were accused under the names of Luther, Zwingli, and the Anabaptists of being “even-hellical” and rebellious. [The Gospel] was hated and shunned and in many places rooted out with severe destruction of life and property, or its introduction was prohibited under pain of such punishment. And so it was that the burdened peasantry had slipped the ropes that bound them, only to be bound with chains.

Document 5

Source: Robert Aske, English gentleman, testimony given before his execution for rebellion against the newly established Protestant regime of Henry VIII, 1537

Once the monasteries in the North [of England] gave great help to poor men and praiseworthy service to God*.

Now no hospitality is shown to travelers. Instead, farmers rent out farms and taverns for profit. Any monies earned from former monastery lands are now going to the King. Also, many tenants who were fed and aided by monasteries now can barely live. Traveling strangers and beggars have no help on the roads. Sea walls, dikes, bridges and high walls that were once maintained by the monasteries for the good of the Commonwealth are now left untended.

*Henry VIII confiscated church lands and closed the monasteries after establishing the Church of England.

Document 6

Source: Ordinance [law] from the Protestant German duchy of Württemberg, 1559

At least twice a year, each pastor shall make in his sermons serious warning to his parishioners that they must be diligent in sending their children to school. And let him stress the great benefit bound to come from this, schools being necessary not only for learning the liberal arts, but also the fear of God, virtue, and discipline. Where the young are neglected and kept out of school, permanent harm, both eternal and earthly, must result, as children grow up without fear and knowledge of God, without discipline, like the dumb beasts of the field, learning nothing about what is needed for their salvation, nor what is useful to them and their neighbors in worldly life.

Document 7

Source: Letter from the Catholic Queen Regent Catarina of Portugal to Count Castanheira, ambassador to France, 1562

From letters that I have now received from my ambassador in the court of the King of France, I have learned of the great role in that realm that the ministers of the Lutheran sect and their followers have, and the regard and authority enjoyed by very important persons in said realm, and how close it is there for the loss of our holy Catholic faith if our Lord [Charles IX of France] does not deal with it.

From the state of these religious questions you will understand how it is our duty to take great care in a remedy for it. Because these religious questions are of the type that they are and that they very much affect the honor of Our Lord and the peace and tranquility of all Christianity, it seems I am obliged to take up this matter with the King of France. I would greatly appreciate you writing to me with all haste if I should do it, and what on this matter I should say to him, for I want to resolve this thing immediately, since to delay could create great harm.

Directions: This question is based on the seven accompanying documents. The documents have been edited for the purpose of this exercise.

 

Document 1

Source: Illustration by Lucas Cranach the Elder, included in a pamphlet by Martin Luther, 1521

 
 
 

Pope Leo X (right) is shown presiding over the collection of indulgences, in contrast to Christ (left) driving the moneylenders out of the temple.

Document 2

Source: Martin Luther, “Temporal Authority: To What Extent It Should be Obeyed,” 1523

If anyone attempted to rule the world by means of the gospel and to abolish all temporal [earthly] law on the plea that all are baptized and Christian and that, according to the gospel there shall be among them no law or sword—or need for either—pray tell me, friend, what would such a person be doing? He would be loosing the ropes and chains of the savage wild beasts and letting them bite and mangle everyone, meanwhile insisting that they are harmless, tame, and gentle creatures. But I would have proof to the contrary in my wounds.

Just so would the wicked, under the name of Christian, abuse religious freedom and carry on their rascality and insist that they were Christians subject neither to earthly law or sword, as some are already ranting and raving.

Document 3

Source: Katharina Schütz Zell, Protestant reformer, Apologia for Master Matthew Zell: Clerical Marriage, 1524

With God’s help I was also the first woman in Strasbourg who opened the way for clerical marriage, when I was then still not consenting or wishing to marry any man. However, since I saw the great fear and furious opposition to clerical marriage, and also the great adultery of the clergy, I myself married a priest with the intention of encouraging and making a way for all Christians—as I hope has also happened. Therefore I also made a little book, in which I showed the foundation of my faith and reason for my marriage, because many people had been greatly amazed by my marriage. For no one had in any way been able to perceive in me, by word or deed, that I wanted to be married.

Document 4

Source: Thomas Müntzer, German Anabaptist, 1525

It is an article of our creed, and one which we wish to realize, that all things are in common, and should be distributed as occasion requires, according to the several necessities of all. Any prince, count, or baron who, after being earnestly reminded of this truth, is still unwilling to accept it, is to be beheaded or hanged.

Document 5

Source: Twelve Articles of the Protestant Peasants of Upper Swabia, Germany, 1525

It is consistent with Scripture that we should be free and should wish to be so. Not that we would wish to be absolutely free and under no authority. God does not teach that we should lead a disorderly life in the lusts of the flesh, but that we should love the Lord our God and our neighbor. He has not commanded us not to obey the authorities, but rather that we should be humble, not only towards those in authority, but towards everyone. We are thus ready to yield obedience according to God’s law to our elected and regular authorities in all proper things becoming to a Christian. We therefore take it for granted that you will release us from serfdom as true Christians, unless it should be shown from the gospel that we are serfs.

Document 6

Source: Nicholas Sander, English Catholic theologian, description of the Protestant Dutch city of Antwerp, 1566

These fresh followers of this new preaching [Protestants] threw down the statues and defaced the painted images, not only of Our Lady [the Virgin Mary] but of all others in the town. They tore the curtains, dashed in pieces the carved work of brass and stone, broke the altars, spoilt the clothes, wrested the irons, pulled up the brass of the gravestones, not sparing the glass and seats which were made about the pillars of the church for men to sit in. These false brethren burned and tore up not only all kind of Church books, but, moreover, destroyed whole libraries of books of all sciences and tongues, yea the Holy Scriptures and the ancient fathers.

Document 7

Source: Florimond de Raemond, French Catholic lawyer, A History of the Heresies in France, published posthumously in 1605

But what purpose do the apostles, priests, and doctors of the church, who according to the Scriptures are ordained of God, serve, if the interpretation of holy writings or the treatment of sacred books by artisans and women are regarded to be as good as those of the ordained? God has given to the church its heralds and ambassadors. They are the only voice it is necessary for us to hear, and not the voices of these villains, strangers or unknowns, trumpets of treason, and furies which hell has vomited forth to drown this miserable century in murders, impieties, filth, and sacrilege.

Directions: This question is based on the seven accompanying documents. The documents have been edited for the purpose of this exercise.

 

Document 1

Source: Samuel von Pufendorf, German philosopher and historian, Of the Law of Nature and Nations, 1672

Monarchy is brought into much narrower Bounds, and under much stricter Ties if, at the first conferring of Sovereignty, it be expressly covenanted between the People and the Prince that the latter shall govern according to certain Fundamental Laws, and in all such Affairs as are not left to his absolute Disposal, shall have recourse to a Council of the Commons, or of the Nobles, and determine nothing without their Consent.

Document 2

Source: John Locke, English Philosopher, Second Treatise of Government, 1690

It is evident, that absolute monarchy, which by some men is counted the only government in the world, is indeed inconsistent with civil society, and so can be no form of civil government at all: for the end of civil society, being to remedy those inconveniences of the state of nature, by setting up a known authority, to which every one of that society may appeal and which every one of the society ought to obey. Wherever any persons are, who have not such an authority to appeal to, there those persons are still in the state of nature; and so is every absolute prince, in respect of those who are under his dominion.

Document 3

Source: Émilie du Châtelet, French author, essay published between 1734 and 1739

Let us reflect briefly on why for so many centuries, not one good tragedy, one good poem, one esteemed history, one beautiful painting, one good book of physics, has come from the hands of women. Let someone give me an explanation, if there is one. I leave it to naturalists to find a physical explanation, but until that happens, women will be entitled to protest against their lack of education. As for me, I confess that if I were kind I would wish to make this scientific experiment. I would reform an abuse that cuts out, so to speak, half of humanity. I would allow women to share the rights of humanity, and most of all to those of the mind.

Document 4

Source: Anonymous, entry for “Tyranny,” Encyclopedia, or a Systematic Dictionary of the Sciences, Arts, and Crafts, France, 1765

A clear distinction must be made between tyranny, which tends to the ruin of the subjects, and a moderate abuse of authority such as may be attributed to human weakness.

In the case of tyranny, it appears that the people have a full right to retake the sovereignty they have entrusted to their leaders, which the latter have abused excessively.

In the case of moderate abuse of authority, it is absolutely the people’s duty to suffer something rather than to rise up by force against their sovereign.

This distinction is founded on the nature of man and government. It is just to suffer patiently the bearable faults of sovereigns, and their light injustices. But as soon as the tyranny is extreme, one has a right to wrest the sacred trust of sovereignty from the tyrant.

Document 5

Source: Denis Diderot, French philosophe, letter to Russian princess Ekaterena Vorontsova-Dashkova, 1771

There is a characteristic spirit for every age. Our own seems to be characterized by the spirit of liberty. The first attack against superstition was violent, excessive. As soon as men dare any sort of assault on the bastion of religion, the most formidable as well as the most respected bastion in existence, there can be no turning back. Once they have looked threateningly upon the majesty of Heaven, they cannot fail, the next instant, to turn their gaze upon those who hold sovereignty on Earth. The cord that binds humanity and keeps it down is made from two strands; one cannot break without the other also giving way.

Document 6

Source: Rabaut Saint-Etienne, French author, commentary on the Act of Tolerance issued by King Louis XVI, 1787

The only thing that non-Catholics gained in the edict of November 1787 was what could not be refused to them. This law, more famous than fair, lays down the ways in which their births, marriages, and deaths should be recorded; it thereby makes it possible for them to be recognized in civil law, and to follow their occupations and professions . . . and that is all it does.

I demand, gentlemen, for all French Protestants, for all the non-Catholics in the kingdom, the same thing that you demand for yourselves: liberty and equal rights. I demand that all French non-Catholics be given the same status as all other citizens in every respect, because they are citizens too, and because law and liberty are impartial.

Document 7

Source: British cartoon satirizing Thomas Paine, “Who Wants Me?” 1792

 
 
 
 
 
 
 

The caption reads: “I am ready and willing to offer my services to any nation or people under heaven who are desirous of liberty and equality.”

Paine holds a scroll showing “Rights of man,” “Common nonsense,” and “Equality of property,” while standing on ribbons that include “loyalty,” “religion,” “protection of property,” and “industry.”

Directions: This question is based on the seven accompanying documents. The documents have been edited for the purpose of this exercise.

 

Document 1

Source: John Trenchard and Thomas Gordon, English political writers, Cato’s Letters, published in the London Journal newspaper, England, 1720

Here is all the precaution which can be taken by human wisdom to make a happy Monarch and a happy People. The Monarch is restrained in nothing, but from doing mischief to his Subjects, and consequently to himself, their true interest being ever the same. And the people can never have any motive to refuse just allegiance to their Monarch whilst the bonds of the Constitution are preserved entire; that is, while parliaments are allowed to meet, and the Courts of Justice remain open. All the Subjects of such a Monarch highly honor and almost worship him.

Document 2

Source: Peter Forsskal, Swedish political writer, “Thoughts on Civil Liberty,” 1759

The more a man may live according to his own inclinations, the more he is free. Therefore, next to life itself, nothing could be more dear to man than freedom. No rational being relinquishes or curtails it unless forced to do so by violence or fear of some greater evil.

However, we often yield to vices and wrongdoing. Thus, boundaries should be set for us, freedom should lose its harmful part, and there should only remain such an amount that, according to one’s innermost will, one may benefit others and oneself, but harm no one.

When this is granted to each and every member of society, then there is true civil liberty.

So, this means that no one is prevented from doing that which is proper and useful for the community, that every honest person may live in safety, obey his conscience, use his property, and contribute to the well-being of his society.

To this liberty, the greatest danger is always posed by those who are the most powerful in the country by dint of their positions, estate, or wealth. Not only do they easily abuse the power they hold, but also constantly increase their rights and strength, so that the other inhabitants must fear them more and more.

Document 3

Source: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, French philosophe, The Social Contract, 1763

Government is wrongly confused with the sovereign, whose agent it is. What then is government? It is an intermediary body established between the subjects and the sovereign to keep them in touch with each other. It is charged with executing the laws and maintaining both civil and political liberty.... The only will dominating government should be the general will or the law. The government’s power is only the public power vested in it. As soon as [government] attempts to let any act come from itself completely independently, it starts to lose its intermediary role. If the time should ever come when the [government] has a particular will of its own stronger than that of the sovereign and makes use of the public power which is in its hands to carry out its own particular will, at that moment the social union will disappear and the body politic will be dissolved.

Document 4

Source: Queen Catherine II (the Great) of Russia, Instruction to the Legislative Commission of 1767

13. What is the true End of Monarchy? Not to deprive People of their natural Liberty; but to correct their Actions, in order to attain the supreme Good.

14. The Form of Government, therefore, which best attains this End, and at the same Time sets less Bounds than others to natural Liberty, is that which coincides with the Views and Purposes of rational Creatures, and answers the End, upon which we ought to fix a steadfast Eye in the Regulations of civil Polity.

16. A Sense of Liberty arises in a People governed by a Monarch; which may produce in these States as much Energy in transacting the most important Affairs, and may contribute as much to the Happiness of the Subjects, as even Liberty itself.

Document 5

Source: Louis-Sebastien Mercier, French playwright, A Scene of Paris, 1781

Religious freedom is entirely possible in Paris; you will never be held accountable for your beliefs. A bishop was once asked: “What are you complaining about? Have you ever seen a single act of sacrilege? Has a single philosopher ever disrupted even one catechism class? Have those who preach from the pulpit ever encountered a single heckler? They have always enjoyed the most gratifying right of all–that of never being interrupted or contradicted whatever they say.” And the bishop replied: “If only God would permit the occasional sacrilege! At least then people would still be thinking about us, but now they can’t even be bothered to show any disrespect.” The Enlightenment has brought us this desirable calm, and fanaticism has been left to consume itself.

Document 6

Source: Moses Mendelssohn, Jerusalem; a Treatise on Ecclesiastical Authority and Judaism, 1783

The state is, if need be, contented with dead works, with services without spirit, with harmony of action without harmony of thought. Even he, who thinks nothing of laws, must do as the law bids, when once it has been sanctioned. The individual citizen can be allowed the privilege of judging of the laws, but not that of acting up to his judgment; for, as a member of society, he was obliged to surrender that right, because without each surrender, a social contract would be a chimera [something impossible to achieve].

Document 7

Source: Pierre Charles Baquoy, French engraver, King Frederick II (the Great) of Prussia visiting Voltaire, image originally created in 1795

 
 
 

Voltaire is seated at left, and Frederick is standing at right.

Evaluate whether or not the revolutions of 1848 were primarily motivated by nationalism.

f.c:
Directions: This question is based on the seven accompanying documents. The documents have been edited for the purpose of this exercise.

 

Document 1

Source: Decree of the French Second Republic issued the day after its establishment, February 1848

The provisional government of the French republic pledges itself to guarantee the means of subsistence of the workingman by labor.

It pledges itself to guarantee labor to all citizens.

It recognizes that workingmen ought to enter into associations among themselves in order to enjoy the advantage of their labor.

The provisional government of the republic decrees the immediate establishment of national workshops.*

*intended to create jobs for unemployed workers

Document 2

Source: List of demands by a group of Hungarian women, Budapest newspaper, April 1848

We demand: that the minister of education shut down as soon as possible every Austrian-controlled girls’ school that stunts the growth of Hungarian pupils with respect to nationality or morals, and establish a model girls’ school at national expense in the capital and in each district.

We demand: that the wealthier Hungarian women effectively promote the instruction of their own offspring and the children of poor people.

We demand: that all true Hungarian women know the most sacred patriotic requirements: to strengthen and assist the general spread of our nationality, which still stands on weak footing in more cultured circles, into every branch of public and private life, and make it a thing of respect and honor not only at home but abroad as well.

Document 3

Source: Honore Daumier, French caricaturist, political cartoon, 1848

Translation of caption: “Victor Hugo and Emile Girardin together attempt to elevate Prince Louis Napoleon on a shield. It’s not very steady!”

Victor Hugo (on the left) was a liberal journalist and novelist. Emile Girardin (on the right) was a conservative newspaper editor and politician. Louis Napoleon, the nephew of Napoleon I, later became Emperor Napoleon III of France after the Revolution of 1848 in France.

Document 4

Source: French socialist pamphlet, France, May 1848

The approaching election will show France and the world if the Revolution must retreat before intrigue and egoism or prove its might by a stunning demonstration of right.

Don’t listen to those who try to persuade to have as your representatives a prince or an heir of the Emperor. . . . Don’t allow yourselves to be blinded by the glow of a name.

Firmly establish the revolution, immutably found the democratic republic with all of its social consequences: this Citizens, should be the goal of our common efforts.

Citizen friends, in the name of your desolated mothers and wives, of your starving children, reinforce the decimated ranks of the Representatives of the democratic and social republic and prove to the world that if the people of France know how to conquer rights, they also know how to keep them.

Document 5

Source: Daniel Manin, lawyer, speech to a crowd in the central square of Venice, 1848

We are free. But it is not enough to have overthrown the old government; we must put another in its place. The right one, I think, is the republic. It will remind us of our past glories improved by modern liberties… We will form one of these centers (in Venice) which must bring about the gradual fusion of Italy into one. Long live the Republic! Long live Liberty!

Document 6

Source: Gustav von Struve: Motion offered to an assembly of German representatives, Frankfurt, March 1848

A long period of the most profound degradation weighs heavily on Germany. The distress of the people has become unbearable. In Upper Silesia it has intensified to the point of famine.

[Therefore we demand]

Abolition of taxes that inhibit Germany’s domestic commerce and agriculture and their replacement: with a progressive income and property tax and with a tariff for the protection of its trade, its industry, and its agriculture;

Elimination of the suffering of the working classes and the middle class, promotion of trade, the business profession, and agriculture.

Rectifying the disproportion between labor and capital by means of a special labor ministry, which shall protect labor, and in particular secure labor a share of the profits created by labor.

Termination of the disunity of Germany.

Termination of the hereditary monarchy (despotism) and its replacement by freely elected parliaments.

Document 7

Source: Giuseppe Mazzini, Italian writer, 1852

The question of nationality can only be resolved by destroying the treaties of 1815 and changing the map of Europe. The question of nationalities, rightly understood, is the alliance of the peoples; the balance of powers based upon new foundations; the organization of the work that Europe has to accomplish.

It was not for a material interest that the people of Vienna fought in 1848. . . . It was not for an increase of wealth that the people of Lombardy fought in the same year. . . . They struggled, they still struggle, as do Poland, Germany, and Hungary, for country and liberty; for a word inscribed upon a banner, proclaiming to the world that they also live, think, love, and labor for the benefit of all.

They speak the same language, they kneel beside the same tombs, they glory in the same tradition; and they demand to associate freely, without obstacles, without foreign domination.

Learning Objective: Explain how and why various groups reacted against the existing order from 1815 to 1914.
Thematic Focus: European states and nations developed governmental and civil institutions from 1450 to the present to organize society and consolidate political power, with a variety of social, cultural, and economic effects.
Historical Development: The revolutions of 1848, triggered by economic hardship and discontent with the political status quo, challenged conservative politicians and governments and led to the breakdown of the Concert of Europe.

Evaluate whether or not the revolutions of 1848 were primarily motivated by nationalism.

f.c:
Directions: This question is based on the seven accompanying documents. The documents have been edited for the purpose of this exercise.

 

Document 1

Source: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, French socialist thinker, letter to Karl Marx (then living in Brussels), 1846

You may still think that no reform is possible at present without a bold stroke, without what was formerly called a revolution… Having myself held this opinion for a long time, I confess now that my more recent works have made me revisit this idea completely.

I see the problem like this: to find a form of economic system that would restore to society the wealth that has been taken from it by another form of economic system. In other words, to turn property against property, in such a way as to establish what you German socialists call community, and which I limited myself to calling liberty, equality. I prefer to burn property with a slow fuse, rather than give it new energy by massacring the property owners.

Document 2

Source: Proclamation of the French Second Republic, February 1848

A reactionary and oligarchical government has just been overthrown by the heroism of the people of Paris.

The blood of the people has flowed as in July [1789]; but this time this courageous people shall not be deceived.

Frenchmen, it is for you to give to the world the example which Paris has given to France; prepare yourselves by order and by confidence in your destiny for the firm institutions which you are about to be called upon to establish.

The unity of the nation, . . . the government of the nation by itself; liberty, equality, and fraternity, these constitute the democratic government which France owes to itself, and which our efforts shall secure for it.

Document 3

Source: Report by a conservative government official in the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, southern Italy, concerning a rural uprising, May 1848

I was met by over 300 of the National Guard, who were preceded by the tricolor flag* and followed by the poor and the young people. Along the road were stationed other leaders of the National Guard. The crowd grew, the number of wretchedly thin and haggard people was in the thousands. Several hundred women with the tricolor flag met us not far from the village. They were dressed in tattered clothes; the very picture of poverty. All of them shouted, “Long live the constitution; long live Italy,” but all they demanded was land to farm and bread.

*a symbol showing support for the unification of Italy

Document 4

Source: Frédéric Bastiat, French economist, journal article, May 1848

Government expenditure [of the new Second Republic] has steadily increased and revenue steadily decreased.

I ask you, what is bound to happen? Capital and production are terrified; they can no longer count on the future. Under the influence of a doctrine like this, capital will hide, flee, and be reduced to nothing. And what will then happen to the workers, these very workers for whom you profess such a lively, sincere, but so unenlightened affection?

And taxes, where will you obtain these? And the financial position, how will this be restored? How are you going to pay the army? How will you pay your debts?

Document 5

Source: Johann Christian Schoeller, Austrian artist, “Metternich’s Exit,” political cartoon, 1848

 
 

The figure on the right is waving the German tricolor flag; the crowd on the left carries a banner that says “Long live the constitution.”

Document 6

Source: The Proclamation of Islaz, a list of demands made by Romanian revolutionaries,* June 1848

The administrative and legislative independence of the Romanian people and non-interference by any outside power in those within it.

Equality of political rights.

Absolute freedom of print.

Equal and complete education for all Romanians of both sexes.

The abolition of the aristocratic ranks.

The abolition, both in fact and in word, of the death penalty.

The convening of a general constituent assembly which will be due to make the country's constitution based on these articles decreed by the Romanian People.

*at the time most Romanians lived under Ottoman rule

Document 7

Source: Appeal of the women of the southern German state of Württemberg to soldiers sent to suppress the revolution, May 1849

Come, now, soldiers of the German states, listen to the call of German women: think of your future, think of the peaceful civilian estate you wish to rejoin one day, think of the peaceful happiness of love and marriage, and of your home.

Hear our oath, which we swear in sacred patriotism:

“Never shall we give our hand at the altar to him whose hand was stained by the blood of his fellow German citizens!”

“Never shall we share our domestic hearth with him who destroyed this—our shrine—with fire and sword!”

“Never shall we approach in faithful love him whose hostile weapon brought misery and destruction upon the German lands!”

Evaluate whether Spanish exploration in the period 1492 to 1600 was motivated primarily by economic considerations or by religious considerations.

f.c:
Directions: This question is based on the seven accompanying documents. The documents have been edited for the purpose of this exercise.

Document 1

 

Source: The Laws of Burgos, created by the Spanish monarchy to regulate Spanish governance of Hispaniola in the Caribbean, 1512

Nothing has sufficed to bring the Indians to a knowledge of our Faith (necessary for their salvation), since by nature they have no manner of virtue or doctrine. The principal obstacle is that their dwellings are remote from the settlements of the Spaniards.

Although, when the Indians go to work for the Spanish settlers, they are taught the things of our Faith, after serving they return to their dwellings where, because of the distance and their own evil inclinations, they immediately forget what they have been taught.

Therefore, for these reasons it was agreed that chiefs and Indians should be brought to dwell near the villages and communities of the Spaniards, so that they may be treated and taught and looked after as is right.

Document 2

Source: Charter granted by Charles I, King of Spain and Holy Roman Emperor, 1518

I have given permission, to Lorenzo de Gorrevod, member of my Council, whereby he, and other authorized authorities, may take to lands in the Americas, discovered and yet undiscovered, four thousand enslaved people from Africa, both male and female, provided that they be Christians, in whatever proportions he may choose.

De Gorrevod and other authorized authorities should make any arrangements with traders or other persons to ship these enslaved peoples, male or female, direct from the isles of Guinea [the west coast Africa] and other regions from which they are accustomed to bring enslaved peoples to our realms and to Portugal, or from any other region they please.

Document 3

Source: Bartolome de Las Casas, Franciscan missionary, treatise written for a debate in Spain on the nature of the Native Americans, 1555

[The Indians have] important kingdoms, large numbers of people who live settled lives in a society, great cities, kings, judges and laws, persons who engage in commerce, buying, selling, lending and the other contracts of the law of nations. Will it not stand proved that my opponent in this debate, the Reverend Doctor Sepúlveda, has spoken wrongly and viciously against people like these, either out of malice or ignorance of Aristotle’s teaching, and, therefore, has falsely and perhaps irreparably slandered them before the entire world?

From the fact that the Indians are barbarians it does not necessarily follow that they are incapable of government. They need not be ruled by others, except to be taught about the Catholic faith and to be admitted to the holy sacraments.

Document 4

Source: Bernal Díaz, Spanish soldier, account of the 1519 expedition to Mexico led by Hernan Cortés, completed in 1568

Cortés explained to the [Aztec emissaries] that we were Christians and vassals of the greatest lord on earth, and that it was at his orders that we had come to this country, because for many years our king had heard rumors about this country and the great prince [Montezuma] who ruled it. He further said that he wished to tell the prince many things in the name of the Emperor, things that would please the prince greatly. Cortés finally said that he wished to trade in good friendship, and he wanted to know where they could meet the prince so they could confer together.

Tendile [one of the emissaries] replied somewhat proudly and said, “You have only just now arrived, and you already ask to speak with our prince. Accept now this present which we give you in his name, and afterwards you will recount to me what you think fitting for me to tell him.”

With that he offered many articles of gold beautifully and richly worked and ten loads of wonderful white cloth made of cotton and feathers. Cortés received it all with smiles in a gracious manner and gave in return beads of twisted glass and other small beads from Spain.

Document 5

Source: Miguel López de Legazpi, governor, proclamation concerning the Muslim population of the island of Panay in the Philippines, conquered by the Spanish in 1569

Under no circumstances whatsoever shall you enslave for profit those inhabitants who have adopted the worship of Mohammad [i.e., who have adopted Islam]. Rather you will attempt to convert them and persuade them to accept our holy faith by good and legitimate means.

Document 6

Source: Richard Hakluyt, Protestant clergyman and English royal official, treatise circulated at the court of Queen Elizabeth I of England, 1584

The harm that Spain’s American treasure caused our country in the time of Charles I, Spanish King and Holy Roman Emperor, who was father to the current emperor and king [Phillip II], should be carefully considered by our queen, out of fear that the continual arrival of more treasure from the Americas to the Spanish kingdom, will cause irrevocable damage to our realm.

With this great treasure did not Charles get from the French king the kingdom of Naples, the Dukedom of Milan, and all other his dominions in Italy, Lombardy, Piedmont, and Savoy? With this treasure did he not take the pope prisoner and sack the pope’s city of Rome? With this treasure did he not take the French king prisoner and maintain wars with France? Indeed, Charles the Emperor employed his treasure to afflict and oppress most of the greatest states of Christendom.

Document 7

Source: Waman Puma de Ayala, Inca nobleman living under Spanish rule, portrayal of a 1532 meeting between Spanish emissaries and the Inca emperor Atahualpa, made in the early 1600s

The Inca emperor is seated in the center. Facing him are a Spanish soldier and a Christian friar holding a religious book. The illustration appeared in Ayala’s chronicle of Peru, in which he criticized Spanish actions.

f.c:
Directions: This question is based on the seven accompanying documents. The documents have been edited for the purpose of this exercise.

Document 1

Source: Christopher Columbus, Genoese explorer in service of the Spanish monarchy, report on his first voyage, sent to the king of Spain and royal officials, 1493

 

In that island which we named Hispaniola [in the Caribbean], there are mountains of very great size and beauty, vast plains, groves, and very fruitful fields, admirably adapted for farming, pasture, and settlement…moreover it abounds in various kinds of spices, gold, and other metals.

In all these islands there is no difference of manners, or of language, but they all clearly understand each other, a circumstance very advantageous for the completion of what I conceive to be the principal wish of our most serene King, namely, the conversion of these people to the holy faith of Christ.

Document 2

Source: Miguel de Estete, Spanish soldier, account of the Spanish conquest of Peru, 1533

We asked why they cared about such a crude and ungainly idol. They were astounded at our daring and defended the honor of their god and said that he was Pachacamac, the Creator, who healed illnesses. From what we could learn, this devil appeared to their priests in that building and spoke with them, and people came with petitions and offerings from the entire kingdom.

Seeing the evil there and the blindness of all those people, we gathered together their leaders and enlightened them. In the presence of all, the building was opened and torn down, and with much solemnity, a tall cross was raised over the spot which for so long the devil had claimed as his own.

Document 3

Source: Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca, Spanish explorer, account of his journeys, 1542

All the inhabitants of Culiacán [in northern Mexico] who were friendly to the Christians and had heard of our arrival, came to visit, bearing beads and feathers. We commanded them to build churches and to bring their principal men to be baptized.

Then our commander made a solemn covenant with God not to enslave any of that region to whom we had guaranteed safety.

Indians came to us shortly with news that many people had returned from the mountains and were living again in the valleys; that they had built churches with crosses and were doing everything we required.

We thank our merciful God that, in the days of Your Majesty's dominion, these nations are all coming voluntarily to Him who created and redeemed us.

Document 4

Source: Francisco Xeres, secretary to Francisco Pizarro, leader of the Spanish conquest of Peru, account of the 1532 meeting with the Inca emperor Atahualpa, 1547

Friar Vicente advanced, with a cross in one hand and the Bible in the other and, going amongst the Inca troops, came to Atahualpa and said: “I am a Priest of God, and I teach Christians the things of God, and in like manner I come to teach you. I beseech you to be their friend, for such is God's will.”

Atahualpa opened the Bible himself, and, without any astonishment at the letters and paper, as had been shown by other Indians, he threw it away. Then he answered with much scorn: “I know well how you have behaved on the road, how you have treated my chiefs, and taken goods from my storehouses. . . . I will not leave this place until they return everything to me.”

Document 5

Source: Michele Soriano, Venetian ambassador to Spain, confidential report to the Venetian government, 1559

The king of Spain gets one-fourth of the whole sum of precious metals [extracted from the Americas], but this is not more than four or five hundred thousand ducats per year [although it is often believed to be much more]. Nor is it likely that this revenue will remain even at this figure. Great quantities of gold and silver are no longer found upon the surface of the earth, and to mine below the surface requires greater effort, skill, and expense. Also, the Indians cannot be forced to mine, because the king has freed them from all obligations of service as soon as they accept the Christian religion. Because of this, it is necessary to acquire slaves from Africa.

Document 6

Source: Unknown Native American artist, portrayal of Hernan Cortés, leader of the Spanish conquest of Mexico, with a column of Spanish soldiers and conscripted Native American laborers, late 1500s

 
 

The banner has a symbol representing the Holy Spirit, part of the Christian trinity. The image appeared in a pictorial record of Aztec history created after the Spanish conquest.

Document 7

Source: Antonio de Berrio, description of an expedition into the interior of northern South America, 1593

The territory is healthy, of moderate temperature, peaceful, fertile, with the fruits of the Indies, much game and fish. Among all the new lands which I have seen, it is the most appropriate for recreation and pleasure. It is extremely rich in gold, and the inhabitants wanted to show me where they mine it.

But in order not to seem greedy, I insisted that my expedition was not undertaken to seek gold but to establish friendship. I only brought back seventeen pieces of worked gold which I sent to the king, and three hatchets of stone which show that, though these people are sometimes barbarous, they do not lack the skills to stop them being so.

q.s: Lorenzo de’ Medici’s interaction with the Duke and Duchess of Milan best illustrates which of the following social and cultural developments in Renaissance Italy?

o.l: The rediscovery and popularization of the classical literary traditions of Greece and Rome
New debates about elite women’s role in the family and in society raised by works such as Baldassare Castiglione’s The Courtier
The success of New Monarchies in centralizing and unifying their states
The rising social prestige of the members of the commercial elite

f.c:
“In July, I went to Milan at the request of the illustrious Duke Galeazzo to stand godfather to his firstborn child. . . . We paid our due to the Duchess by presenting her with a necklace of gold and a large diamond, which cost near 2,000 [Venetian] ducats. The consequence was that the said Lord desired that I should stand godfather to all his children. . . .

To do as others had done, I held a joust in the Piazza Santa Croce [in Florence] at great expense and with great pomp. I think we spent about 10,000 ducats on that and, although I was not highly versed in the use of weapons and the delivery of blows, the first prize was given to me. . . .

Piero, our father, departed this life on July 2. . . . I find that from 1434 till now [our family] has spent large sums of money, as appear in a small notebook [found among my father’s possessions]. Incredible are the sums written down. They amount to 663,755 [Florentine] florins given for alms, buildings, and taxes, let alone other expenses. But I do not regret this, for though many would consider it better to have that sum in their purse, I consider that it gave great honor to our State, and I think the money was well expended.”

q.ex: The Black Death of the mid-14th century killed approximately one-third of Europe's population, which temporarily improved conditions for surviving peasants due to labor shortages that gave them greater bargaining power. As population recovered in the 15th and 16th centuries, the labor surplus shifted power back to landowners, who sought to reimpose stricter feudal obligations and reduce peasant freedoms. This demographic recovery created increased competition for land and resources, allowing lords to demand more from peasants while offering less in return. The resulting economic pressures and attempts by lords to restore pre-plague conditions generated significant tensions that contributed to peasant unrest and demands for reform. Option i1

European countries undertook major infrastructure projects during the 1930s as a direct response to the Great Depression, which began with the 1929 stock market crash and caused massive unemployment and economic contraction across Europe. Governments adopted interventionist policies, including public works programs, to create jobs, stimulate demand, and revive their economies. These infrastructure projects, such as road construction, dam building, and other large-scale public works, were designed to put unemployed workers back to work while simultaneously modernizing national infrastructure. This approach was consistent with Keynesian economic theory, which advocated for government spending during economic downturns to counteract the effects of depression.

Evaluate whether the collapse of communism was primarily caused by factors outside the Soviet bloc or by factors within the Soviet bloc.

f.c:
This question is based on the accompanying documents. The documents have been edited for the purpose of this exercise. Using the document, evaluate whether the collapse of communism was primarily caused by factors outside the Soviet bloc or by factors within the Soviet bloc.

 

 

Document 1

Source: Adam Michnik, Polish intellectual living in exile in Paris, “A New Evolutionism,” essay in an English-language journal published by the International Association for Cultural Freedom, an anticommunist group financed by the United States Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), 1976.

We must clearly define our own attitude towards the conflict between Polish workers and the Polish communist government that is taking place now. We must choose between the point of view of the oppressor and that of the oppressed. By showing our solidarity with the workers on strike, with demonstrating students or dissident intellectuals, we are rejecting the views of those who believe that our problems can be solved by acting within the Communist Party, or making concessions to the Communist Party. In my opinion, the only possibility for dissidents in Eastern Europe is an unceasing struggle for reforms that will extend civil liberties and guarantee respect for human rights.

The specter of Soviet intervention, of Soviet tanks in the streets of Warsaw often paralyzes the will to resist. The memories of Budapest in 1956 and Prague in 1968 seem to reinforce the widespread conviction that the rulers of the USSR will prevent any change. But that is actually not necessarily true. For the Soviet leaders, the memory of the international repercussions of their interventions in Hungary and Czechoslovakia is still fresh. They must also realize that for the Soviets a decision to intervene militarily in Poland would literally mean war. Militarily we Poles would lose such a war, but it would bring no political victory to the Soviet Union. It would be a national massacre for Poland, but also a political defeat for the Soviet Union. That is why it is possible to imagine that the leaders of the USSR and Poland would do everything they can to avoid a direct intervention.

 

Document 2

Source: Károly Király, vice president of a Communist Party-controlled organization representing ethnic Hungarians in Romania, letter to a fellow party leader, 1978. The letter was smuggled out of Romania and published in The New York Times.

It is an open secret that in cities in Romania where the majority of the population is ethnically Hungarian, Romanians who speak no Hungarian are being appointed as mayors. Use of our native Hungarian language is severely restricted at Communist Party meetings. Signs identifying institutions and localities in the native Hungarian of the population have almost completely disappeared. The replacement of Hungarian-speaking state officials (where there still are any) with Romanians is being carried out with incredible persistence, to the point where in cities that are almost entirely Hungarian, there is not a single Party secretary that is ethnically Hungarian.

It is clear that many aspects of this reality violate both the Constitution of Romania and our Party’s founding charter and fundamental principles. What is occurring has nothing in common with Marxism-Leninism, fundamental human rights, or human dignity—all those things that are trumpeted far and wide in our Party propaganda. This tendency to forcefully assimilate the minorities living in Romania casts doubts over the sincerity of all our policies in general and, for millions of citizens, it destroys their confidence in socialist society.

I am writing to you with a deep sense of responsibility, as I am one of those Communists who is convinced of the truth of our ideals. I have fought for these ideals since my tender youth and later as a member of Party and state leadership as well. But without a just and real solution of the nationalities question, the new society, the socialism that we all want, can never be built up.

Document 4

Source: Vera F. K., mother of a Soviet army soldier killed in action in Afghanistan,* interview with journalist and oral historian Svetlana Alexievich, late 1980s.

Was it necessary to send boys, like my Kolya, to Afghanistan? My neighbor kept telling me—“Couldn’t you scrape together a couple of thousand rubles and bribe someone?” We knew a woman who did exactly that, and kept her son out. I didn’t realize I could save my son with money. I thought the best gift I could give him was a decent upbringing.

“We are going to give you an apartment, for your son’s sacrifice,” I was promised by the local party authorities shortly after he was killed. “You can choose any empty apartment in the area.” So I found one in the city center, in a building made of proper brick, not poor-quality prefab concrete like the rest of them, with a nice modern layout. I went back to the town hall with the address. “Are you out of your mind? That block is strictly for District Communist Party committee members!” Is my son’s blood that much cheaper than theirs?

*The Soviet Union’s military intervention in Afghanistan lasted from 1979 to 1989. The intervention was met by resistance from fighters backed by the United States and other nations.

Perhaps the most important factor that will govern how Moscow reacts to the Strategic Defense Initiative involves the question of Soviet financial resource constraints and the inevitable difficulties that will arise as the Soviets attempt to grapple with this challenge. After two decades of armed forces expansion, the Soviets are now finding themselves more and more saddled with real limits to attainable military growth. To deal with this problem, [Soviet leader] Gorbachev has proposed greater investment in civilian technologies, particularly those concerned with electronic engineering, machine tools, computers and instruments.
